samasa.vigraha: एकम् अग्रं यस्य तत् एकाग्रम्; एकाग्रं हृदयम् एकाग्रहृदयम्; तस्मिन् स्थितः
samasa.type: saptamī tatpuruṣa containing a karmadhāraya (एकाग्रहृदय) whose first member एकाग्र is a bahuvrīhi
samasa.literal: standing in a heart that has one point
samasa.sense: with his whole mind gathered on her
samasa.alt: Or tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa, एकाग्रहृदयेन स्थितः ‘standing (there) with a concentrated heart’; the sense — Brahmā’s focused devotion — is the same.

samasa.type: upapada tatpuruṣa (traditional etymology; अर्दन from √अर्द् ‘to afflict, stir’)
samasa.alt: Traditional etymologies differ (also ‘he whom people entreat’, from √अर्द् ‘to ask’); the name is used here simply for Viṣṇu.

morph.note: Perfect of √स्तु: the reduplicated syllable keeps the stop (tu-), and the s of the root becomes ṣ, drawing t into ṭ (tu-ṣṭāva); the root vowel takes vṛddhi in the 3rd singular. The verb that frames the whole hymn (1.73–87).
Absolutive of √दृश्: दृश् + त्वा → दृष्ट्वा (ś → ṣ, t → ṭ). Its subject is Brahmā, the subject of तुष्टाव.
Past participle of प्र + √स्वप् with samprasāraṇa (स्वप् → सुप्): ‘deeply asleep’.

mantras.anvaya: (सः ब्रह्मा) तौ उग्रौ असुरौ च प्रसुप्तं जनार्दनं च दृष्ट्वा एकाग्रहृदयस्थितः तां योगनिद्रां तुष्टाव।
mantras.anvaya_en: The subject (ब्रह्मा) comes from 1.68; an absolutive phrase with two objects joined by च … च, then the main verb with its object.
mantras.lit: having seen both those two fierce asuras and Janārdana fast asleep, praised that Yoganidrā, steadied in a one-pointed heart —
mantras.tr: seeing the two fierce asuras and Janārdana deep in sleep, with his heart wholly gathered, began to praise Yoganidrā —

comm.t: Brahmā sees the danger and sees that Viṣṇu cannot help while asleep. With a one-pointed heart he praises Yoganidrā, the power holding Viṣṇu — the hymn of 1.73–87.
The narrative logic is precise: to wake Viṣṇu, Brahmā addresses not Viṣṇu but the sleep that holds him. In the Śākta reading even the highest god’s activity depends on her release.

morph.note: धात्री is the feminine of the agent noun धातृ (√धा + tṛc), formed with ṅīp: ‘she who places, supports’.
Feminine of the -in agent noun कारिन् (+ ī): कारिणी, accusative कारिणीम्. Compare the masculine instrumental कारिणा in 1.54.

mantras.anvaya: (ब्रह्मा) हरेः विबोधनार्थाय हरिनेत्रकृतालयां विश्वेश्वरीं जगद्धात्रीं स्थितिसंहारकारिणीं (तां योगनिद्रां तुष्टाव)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A string of accusative epithets in apposition to योगनिद्राम् (1.69), with a dative of purpose; the verb is तुष्टाव (1.69).
mantras.lit: for the sake of the awakening of Hari — (her) who had made her abode in Hari’s eyes, the sovereign of the universe, the supporter of the world, the maker of maintenance and dissolution,
mantras.tr: to wake Hari: she who dwelt in Hari’s eyes, sovereign of the universe, sustainer of the world, who preserves it and dissolves it —

comm.t: The purpose of Brahmā’s praise is stated — to wake Hari — and the Goddess is described by her place (resting in Viṣṇu’s eyes, as sleep) and her cosmic functions: sovereign, supporter, preserver and dissolver of the world.
The epithets already give her the works usually divided among the gods: preservation (Viṣṇu’s) and dissolution (Rudra’s). The hymn will add creation (1.75–77), so that all three belong to her.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same epithet, name 935, जगद्धात्री, and lists the three functions as separate names: 264, सृष्टिकर्त्री; 266, गोप्त्री; 268, संहारिणी.

samasa.literal: she who has no equal measure

morph.note: Genitive singular of the s-stem तेजस्; its construction is open (see flags): with प्रभुः ‘lord of radiance’, or with अतुलाम् ‘unequalled in radiance’.

mantras.anvaya: तेजसः प्रभुः (ब्रह्मा) विष्णोः अतुलां भगवतीं निद्रां (तुष्टाव)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The half-verse closes the sentence begun in 1.68: more accusatives in apposition to योगनिद्राम्, and the nominative प्रभुः restating the subject.
mantras.lit: — the Blessed Sleep of Viṣṇu, the incomparable — (so) the lord of radiance (praised her).
mantras.tr: the incomparable Lady, the Sleep of Viṣṇu. So Brahmā, lord of splendour, praised her.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Brahmā’ and ‘praised her’ are supplied from 1.68–69 to close the sentence.

comm.t: The last epithets: she is Viṣṇu’s Sleep, the Blessed One, beyond compare. The nominative प्रभुः restates the subject, Brahmā, before the hymn begins.
The Goddess is named here by her plainest name, निद्रा ‘sleep’, with the honorific भगवती: what holds the highest god is not a lesser power but the Blessed One herself.

flags.uncertain: The construction of तेजसः is open. Taken here with प्रभुः, ‘the lord of radiance’, an epithet of Brahmā (the subject); it can also be read with अतुलाम्, ‘(her) unequalled in radiance’, with प्रभुः simply ‘the Lord’. Both are grammatical; the sense of the verse is not affected.

comm.t: Within the sage Medhas’s narration, Brahmā on the navel-lotus speaks to Yoganidrā. His hymn (1.73–87) is the first of the four great hymns of the Devī Māhātmya.

sandhi.note: Before s the visarga may stay (as printed) or become s; the Gita Press keeps the visarga.

samasa.type: tatpuruṣa with कार ‘making, utterance’ after a quoted sound (as in ओंकार)
samasa.sense: the cry vaṣaṭ with which the hotṛ priest signals the pouring of the oblation
she whose nature is sacred sound — the accent of the Veda, or the vowel that makes speech audible
samasa.alt: स्वर can mean the Vedic accent (udātta, anudātta, svarita), a vowel, or a musical note; the verse does not say which. The Vedic sense suits the ritual words before it.

morph.note: Bahuvrīhis ending in आत्मन् add -ka; in the feminine the a before -kā becomes i: आत्मक → आत्मिका. The same formation recurs as मात्रात्मिका in 1.74.
A masculine noun predicated of the Goddess: in identity statements (‘you are X’) the predicate noun keeps its own gender.

mantras.anvaya: त्वं स्वाहा, त्वं स्वधा, त्वं हि स्वरात्मिका वषट्कारः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three identity statements with त्वम् repeated; स्वरात्मिका qualifies the subject.
mantras.lit: You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, you indeed are the vaṣaṭ-call, you whose self is sound.
mantras.tr: You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā; you are the sacred cry Vaṣaṭ — your very self is the sound of the Veda.

comm.t: Brahmā opens by identifying the Goddess with the three ritual calls of Vedic sacrifice: svāhā (offering to the gods), svadhā (offering to the ancestors) and vaṣaṭ (the hotṛ’s call at the oblation). She is the very sound through which offering reaches its recipient.

The hymn begins with sacrificial speech because in the Vedic view the sacrifice sustains the world. To call her svāhā and svadhā is to make her the power by which gods and ancestors are fed — the support of both worlds. In Purāṇic myth Svāhā and Svadhā are also personified as goddesses, consorts of Agni and of the ancestors.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same pair as consecutive names: 535, स्वाहा, and 536, स्वधा.
